claim: 173 high-quality SARS-CoV-2 genomes were obtained from patients and healthcare workers across multiple geographically distinct UK hospitals.
source: We sequenced SARS-CoV-2 genomes for patients and healthcare workers (HCWs) across multiple geographically distinct UK hospitals, obtaining 173 high-quality SARS-CoV-2 genomes.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the number of genomes obtained and their sources.

claim: Eight patient contact clusters (PCCs) were identified with significantly increased similarity in genomic variants compared to non-clustered samples.
source: We identified eight patient contact clusters (PCC) with significantly increased similarity in genomic variants compared to non-clustered samples.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the identification of eight PCCs with statistical significance.

claim: Incorporation of HCW location data increased the number of individuals within PCCs and identified additional links in SARS-CoV-2 transmission pathways.
source: Incorporation of HCW location further increased the number of individuals within PCCs and identified additional links in SARS-CoV-2 transmission pathways.
evidence: The manuscript directly states the effect of incorporating HCW location data.

claim: Patients within PCCs carried viruses more genetically identical to HCWs in the same ward location.
source: Patients within PCCs carried viruses more genetically identical to HCWs in the same ward location.
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states this finding about genetic similarity.

claim: The SARS-CoV-2 pandemic continues to place a significant burden on healthcare services worldwide.
source: The severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus-2 (SARS-CoV-2) pandemic continues to place a significant burden on healthcare services worldwide (Miller et al., 2020; Propper et al., 2020; Maringe et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three published studies.

claim: Individuals at high risk of developing severe responses to SARS-CoV-2 infection are vulnerable to transmission in hospitals and care homes due to close and regular contact between patients and healthcare workers.
source: Reducing the spread and outbreak of SARS-CoV-2 infections is particularly important in hospitals and care homes where individuals at high risk of developing severe responses to infection are vulnerable to transmission due to close and regular contact between patients and healthcare workers (HCWs) (Clark et al., 2020; Nguyen et al., 2020; Rivett et al., 2020).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies.

claim: SARS-CoV-2 vaccines may reduce risk to individuals in hospitals who receive the vaccine.
source: Whilst the recent development of promising SARS-CoV-2 vaccines may reduce risk to individuals in hospitals who receive the vaccine (Walsh et al., 2020; Anderson et al., 2020; Keech et al., 2020; Lodge, 2020), risk of infection will not be completely mitigated.
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to four studies on vaccines.

claim: Risk of SARS-CoV-2 infection will not be completely mitigated by vaccines.
source: Whilst the recent development of promising SARS-CoV-2 vaccines may reduce risk to individuals in hospitals who receive the vaccine (Walsh et al., 2020; Anderson et al., 2020; Keech et al., 2020; Lodge, 2020), risk of infection will not be completely mitigated.
evidence: This is a speculative statement about the limitations of vaccines.

claim: Standard methods of infection control will continue to be required to ensure patient and HCW safety.
source: Standard methods of infection control will continue to be required to ensure patient and HCW safety.
evidence: This is an inference based on the statement that vaccines will not completely mitigate risk.

claim: Regular and iterative testing for SARS-CoV-2 in both patients and HCWs underpins approaches that quantify and control nosocomial transmission.
source: Regular and iterative testing for SARS-CoV-2, in both patients and HCWs, underpins approaches that quantify and control nosocomial transmission (Black et al., 2020) but will not provide insights into how the virus may have spread throughout an institution, alone.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Black et al., 2020.

claim: Testing alone will not provide insights into how SARS-CoV-2 may have spread throughout an institution.
source: Regular and iterative testing for SARS-CoV-2, in both patients and HCWs, underpins approaches that quantify and control nosocomial transmission (Black et al., 2020) but will not provide insights into how the virus may have spread throughout an institution, alone.
evidence: This is an inference about the limitations of testing without additional data.

claim: The degree to which different groups (patients, HCW) propagate SARS-CoV-2 transmission remains uncertain.
source: Since the degree to which different groups (patients, HCW) propagate SARS-CoV-2 transmission remains uncertain, the utility of screening approaches to prospectively prevent nosocomial spread is difficult to evaluate.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: HCWs are an important component in pathogen outbreak investigations.
source: It is well established that HCWs are an important component in pathogen outbreak investigations (Peacock et al., 2018; Wenger et al., 1995; de Swart et al., 2000).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to three studies and described as well established.

claim: 39 (23%) of the 173 high-quality sequenced samples were from HCWs.
source: Of the 173 high-quality sequenced samples, 39 (23%) were HCW samples.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts and percentages from the study data.

claim: 134 samples were collected from patients admitted to a total of 31 wards and units situated across five hospitals.
source: The remaining 134 samples were collected from patients admitted to a total of 31 wards and units situated across the five hospitals.

claim: Samples consistently met 10× minimum coverage thresholds when a total yield of >400 ng was obtained.

claim: Samples with Ct values of 31 or more resulted in lower amplicon yield and frequently failed to meet sequencing coverage thresholds.

evidence: The manuscript provides specific Ct value thresholds and references Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: 268 genomic variants were identified in the 173 high-quality samples in comparison to MN908947.3.
source: In the 173 high-quality samples, we identified 268 genomic variants in comparison to MN908947.3, of which 86 were recurrent variants across samples (range = 2–126 samples) and 182 were unique to single samples.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of genomic variants identified.

claim: 86 of the 268 genomic variants were recurrent variants across samples (range = 2–126 samples).
source: In the 173 high-quality samples, we identified 268 genomic variants in comparison to MN908947.3, of which 86 were recurrent variants across samples (range = 2–126 samples) and 182 were unique to single samples.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of recurrent variants.

claim: 182 of the 268 genomic variants were unique to single samples.
source: In the 173 high-quality samples, we identified 268 genomic variants in comparison to MN908947.3, of which 86 were recurrent variants across samples (range = 2–126 samples) and 182 were unique to single samples.
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts of unique variants.

source: Eight-seven percent (151/173) of sequenced genomes were confidently assigned to an existing lineage (SH-alrt > 80%, UFbootstrap > 90%).

claim: 71% (122/173) of viral genomes were assigned to lineage B.1.1.
source: We identified 11 distinct lineages in our cohort, with a bias towards viral genomes assigned to lineage B.1.1 (71%, 122/173; Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific percentages and counts for lineage B.1.1.

claim: There were no samples assigned to lineage A.
source: There were no samples assigned to lineage A.

claim: Viral lineage B.1.1 showed a constant relative frequency over time.
source: Incorporating the calendar week of sample collection into this analysis suggested a constant relative frequency of viral lineage B.1.1 over time (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).

claim: Viral lineage B.1.1 was present in samples collected from 29 different wards, including A and E, and in HCWs.

claim: Viral lineage B.1.1 was present in the cohort between calendar weeks 12–23.

source: We observed clusters within the phylogenetic tree that were formed predominantly from viral genome sequences taken in individual wards (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).

claim: 19/31 of the samples in one identified cluster were collected from a single hospital ward (H2_W7).
source: For example, 19/31 of the samples in one of these identified clusters were collected from a single hospital ward (H2_W7, Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: The manuscript provides specific counts for a cluster and references Figure 1—figure supplement 3.

source: The phylogenetic clusters were supported by maximum-likelihood and consensus (10,000 ultrafast bootstraps) approaches for tree creation.

evidence: The manuscript provides specific fold-change values from statistical analysis.

claim: Significantly increased genetic similarity was identified in viral samples between patients and HCWs in the same ward locations in comparison to patients and HCWs from different wards (p<0.001).

source: For example, in PCC_B and PCC_D (Figure 3), which occurred on the same hospital ward at different time points, the original 'founder' viral samples contained the novel (at time of sample collection) genomic variant MN908947.3–3228-T-G.

claim: The number of genomic variants identified against the MN908947.3 reference genome increases over time within each of the contact networks.
source: We observed further trends indicative of nosocomial outbreaks, including the number of genomic variants identified against the MN908947.3 reference genome increasing over time within each of the contact networks, and consistently observed that samples collected early during the suspected outbreaks had a greater number of derived or identical samples within the outbreak than those collected at a later day (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal trends observed in the data and references Figure 3.

claim: Samples collected early during the suspected outbreaks had a greater number of derived or identical samples within the outbreak than those collected at a later day.
source: We observed further trends indicative of nosocomial outbreaks, including the number of genomic variants identified against the MN908947.3 reference genome increasing over time within each of the contact networks, and consistently observed that samples collected early during the suspected outbreaks had a greater number of derived or identical samples within the outbreak than those collected at a later day (Figure 3).
evidence: The manuscript describes temporal trends observed in the data and references Figure 3.

claim: The observed temporal trends would be expected if single ancestral SARS-CoV-2 sequences were original founders of an outbreak.
source: Both of these trends would be expected if single ancestral SARS-CoV-2 sequences were original founders of an outbreak.

claim: Inclusion of contact data increased confidence in the characterisation of nosocomial outbreaks.

source: This strategy, in combination with additional infection control measures such as staff bubbles, is widespread as a method to reduce nosocomial infection.

source: Viral genome sequencing offers a realistic possibility to track and identify root causes of nosocomial transmissions (Lucey et al., 2020; Meredith et al., 2020).

source: It has been previously noted that the low genetic diversity of SARS-CoV-2 causes complexity in the identification of nosocomial outbreaks, as samples may be genetically identical by chance rather than through transmission between individuals (Meredith et al., 2020; Gudbjartsson et al., 2020).

claim: The data reemphasize the low genetic diversity of SARS-CoV-2, with a median number of 11 (range = 2–16) variants identified per sample.

claim: The average pairwise similarity of viral samples was 61.5%.
source: Our data reemphasise this low genetic diversity of SARS-CoV-2, with a median number of 11 (range = 2–16) variants identified per sample, and an average pairwise similarity of 61.5% (Figure 2).

claim: Location of staff workplaces was available for 31/39 HCWs.

claim: Individuals who had been in contact during the likely period of infection were more likely to have genetically more similar viral samples than individuals who had not been in contact.
source: These analyses confirmed that individuals who had been in contact during this period were more likely to have genetically more similar viral samples than individuals who had not been in contact (Figure 2).

claim: Viral samples may be genetically identical or similar by chance due to the low genetic diversity of SARS-CoV-2.
source: While we cannot exclude that viral samples are genetically identical or similar by chance due to the low genetic diversity of SARS-CoV-2, the spatial and temporal patterns of viral genetic relatedness that we observe provide strong evidence for nosocomial transmission amongst both patients and HCWs.
evidence: This acknowledges a limitation based on known properties of SARS-CoV-2.

claim: The spatial and temporal patterns of viral genetic relatedness provide strong evidence for nosocomial transmission amongst both patients and HCWs.
source: While we cannot exclude that viral samples are genetically identical or similar by chance due to the low genetic diversity of SARS-CoV-2, the spatial and temporal patterns of viral genetic relatedness that we observe provide strong evidence for nosocomial transmission amongst both patients and HCWs.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed patterns in the data.

claim: Spatial and temporal patterns of viral genetic relatedness are observed in at least five distinct clusters, across three geographically distinct hospitals.
source: These trends are observed in at least five distinct clusters, across three geographically distinct hospitals.

claim: The presence of novel genomic variants (at the time of analysis) transmitting through identified clusters further reinforces evidence for nosocomial transmission.

claim: The data support the widespread adoption of iterative screening strategies for HCWs who may be pre-symptomatic or asymptomatic shedders of SARS-CoV-2.
